look_here_first: FIRST recognize the pale FEATHERY cluster of narrow one-sided racemes arising close together at the tip of ONE flowering stem (commonly 4–20 branches in Flora of North America). THEN inspect an actual detached mature floret for the conspicuous distal tuft of fine fertile-lemma hairs and its separate awn. To compare with C. verticillata, look for separated head whorls; to compare with C. cucullata, dissect the inflated sterile hood. A head silhouette alone is not a certain species identification.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Accepted POWO species with Texas state-level native distribution; approved iNaturalist source pool; project three-county target-zone criterion not independently verified.

morphology_keys.habit: Tufted annual grass of disturbed places with terminal digitate panicle; racemes often 5–10 cm.
morphology_keys.spikelets: Fertile lemma about 2.5–4.2 mm, with long apical marginal hairs (>1.5 mm) and awn about 2.5–15 mm; one or two reduced sterile florets.
best_field_traits: Racemes mostly in one terminal whorl
Conspicuous long hairs on apical fertile lemma margins
crew_field_walkthrough: Photograph the complete terminal fan and central point where long pale racemes join.
Inspect the second closeup for the visible spikelet-bearing rachis and pointed parts; do not assume the points are hairs from a particular lemma.
Expose basal root crown and isolate one mature fertile lemma to demonstrate long apical hairs with mm scale; compare with C. verticillata's whorled architecture.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Entire terminal fan in flowering plant context, noting any lower distinct whorls.
Basal crown with root and nodes showing annual character.
Mature fertile floret at scale with the true crown of 1.5–4 mm hairs.
One or two mature sterile florets and awns, clear separate measurements.
crew_field_steps: Start with the striking densely grouped pale terminal fan in the first picture; the branches rise together near the top.
The second photo shows awnlike projecting structures along a spike-bearing branch. This teaches what to magnify, not a definitive measurement of the fertile-lemma hair crown.

comparisons.key_distinctions: C. virgata often has a single terminal digitate fan of feathery racemes, while verticillata has well-separated tiers and may form a tumbling mature head. C. cucullata has shorter crowded whorls and the strongly inflated sterile hood. Fertile-lemma apical hair crown, awn and annual crown are needed for confident C. virgata.
comparisons.cautions: Do not certify county nativity from a disturbed-site iNaturalist observation; do not infer identification from digitate head or color alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: How to identify Chloris virgata in the field
steps: 1 · THE HEAD — Look at Matt Lavin's attached compact featherlike terminal head (image 0, first teaching panel). It is a seedhead photograph, not an entire rooted plant. Check for a cluster of one-sided racemes arising near one tip; photograph ALL insertion levels on a single unbroken culm.

2 · THE SPIKELET ROWS — Compare the Augusto Olmos Mercado and Harry Rose raceme macros (source images 1 and 3). Actual packed spikelets and slender projections are visible, but do not call every projection a fertile-lemma hair or measure with fingers.

3 · THE FINE HAIR CROWN — Examine Jim Conrad's true detached floret macro (source image 7) and Harry Rose's awned detached macro (source image 5). Long stiff awns and a spreading tuft of many much finer pale hairs are visible. Their separate insertion points and lengths still need a calibrated dissection.

4 · THE BASE — Jim Conrad's dry-reservoir whole-ground context (source image 8) shows culms converging at a central basal region, NOT exposed fibrous roots. Do not claim a photographed annual root system. In the field lift one attached plant, expose the fibrous crown and all tillers, and note whether a decumbent stem is rooted at an individual node.

5 · THE INNER LIGULE — Harry Rose's sheath photo (source image 2) shows where the blade leaves the sheath but cannot reliably resolve the free ciliate/erose membrane. Separate its actual edge from sheath rim, split tissues and unrelated long collar hairs; photograph the opened junction with 1-mm scale. Published ligule ranges vary by treatment.

6 · THE OTHER WINDBREAKERS — Compare real C. verticillata photos for racemes at multiple separate heights; compare C. cucullata at dissected spikelet level for its rounded sterile lemma. C. virgata is usually tufted and annual by FNA but may root along a lower stem; neither annuality nor an underground rhizome can be proved by a head-only photograph.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: C. virgata often has a single terminal digitate fan of feathery racemes, while verticillata has well-separated tiers and may form a tumbling mature head. C. cucullata has shorter crowded whorls and the strongly inflated sterile hood. Fertile-lemma apical hair crown, awn and annual crown are needed for confident C. virgata.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Field-ID and photo-rights review verified existing archived images and gross arrows. The 9 archived JPEGs include an attached head, actual floret macros, a ground-level base with roots HIDDEN, and a collar search view with unmeasured ligule. Do not count the head image as a whole rooted plant, and do not call the sheath lip a ligule or infer root emergence at a basal node. Zero new image bytes/arrows in this pass.

Do not force a single 0.2–1 mm limit on every specimen. Photograph an opened junction side-on and face-on beside a true 1-mm ruler.

field_id_finish_pass.stage: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — feather fan and bristly branch visible; fertile-lemma crown and annual base not photographed
field_id_finish_pass.recognition: Feather fingergrass often forms a TIGHT TERMINAL FAN of about 4–20 radiating, feathery-looking racemes on an annual tuft. Under a lens the fertile lemma typically has a distinctive crown of long apical hairs (about 1.5–4 mm) and a long awn. Current pictures show the feathery head and visible bristly units, NOT a measured isolated fertile lemma or proof of annual crown.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalikes: C. virgata often has a single terminal digitate fan of feathery racemes, while verticillata has well-separated tiers and may form a tumbling mature head. C. cucullata has shorter crowded whorls and the strongly inflated sterile hood. Fertile-lemma apical hair crown, awn and annual crown are needed for confident C. virgata.
what_to_photograph: Entire terminal fan in flowering plant context, noting any lower distinct whorls.
Basal crown with root and nodes showing annual character.
Mature fertile floret at scale with the true crown of 1.5–4 mm hairs.
One or two mature sterile florets and awns, clear separate measurements.
field_id_finish_pass.photo_review: Original pixels of all selected local photos were examined, arrows on actual visible parts only.
field_id_finish_pass.public_release: GitHub content commit does not prove Pages deployment.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.look_here_first: FEATHER FINGERGRASS: trace the feathery head to a mostly terminal cluster of 3–15 (often 6–14) fingerlike racemes on an annual crown. Under a lens confirm the fertile lemma's distinct crown of 1.5–4 mm apical hairs and a long subapical awn; the plume alone is not species proof.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.growth_form: Usually tufted annual with decumbent or ascending basal culms, often 10–80 cm in southwestern US treatment; no perennial rhizome. Lower nodes may occasionally root, so rooting at a node does not automatically make this a perennial.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.ligule_collar: Ligule a short, irregularly lacerate, ciliate MEMBRANE approximately 0.2–1 mm in southwestern US treatment. Sheath commonly smooth and keeled; photograph true membrane separately from adjacent blade hairs with 1-mm scale.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.flowering_architecture: Several to many (about 3–15) slender racemes crowded into a terminal digitate or subdigitate fan, each often 3–9 cm; featherlike texture comes from floret awns and hairs, not generic spikelet bristles.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.spikelet_glumes: Laterally compressed, one fertile floret with one or two reduced sterile upper florets. Mature spikelet approximately 2.5–4.5 mm; lower glume usually 1.5–2.5 mm, upper 2.5–4.5 mm, typically 1-veined and keeled. Upper glume can taper to a short awn or awnlike point: do NOT claim both glumes universally awnless.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.lemma_palea_awn: Fertile lemma body approximately 2.5–4 mm, three-veined, with 1.5–4 mm apical/marginal hair crown and a subapical awn approximately 5–15 mm. Reduced sterile upper lemma(s) may bear a separate awn approximately 5–12 mm. The hair crown, fertile lemma awn and sterile lemma awn are three different structures; annotate only when visually distinguishable.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.central_texas_lookalikes: C. verticillata has racemes on separated tiers along the flowering axis rather than a compact terminal fan; C. cucullata has short crowded whorls and inflated hoodlike sterile lemma; C. andropogonoides has longer slender arms. A source-reported Chloris hybrid may confound silhouettes. Compare mature lemma hair crowns and awns, not color alone.
precise_last_mile_photo_arrow_gaps: Same locally identified annual with roots, whole stem and terminal raceme fan, centimeter ruler; document any lower separate whorls.
True 0.2–1 mm ciliate membrane on attached leaf-sheath collar at 10–20× and 1-mm scale.
One mature intact spikelet at 10–20× showing lower and upper glumes, with any upper-glume point separately identified.
Separated fertile lemma with 1.5–4 mm hair crown and its 5–15 mm awn, plus distinct reduced sterile upper lemma and its awn, each measured.
Same-scale C. verticillata and C. cucullata flowering axes and lemma anatomy; do not draw arrows on features unresolved in two existing photos.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.existing_evidence: Two existing species photographs show a feathery head and gross branch architecture, not measured fertile lemma crown, sterile lemma, true ligule or rooted annual base; preserve original arrow positions and source rights.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Pale feathery fan at one terminal hub; verify the hair crown
field_id_short_tiles.details: Begin with the photographed attached terminal cluster (panel 0): many narrow, one-sided racemes arise close together near one flowering-stem tip and appear pale and feathery. Flora of North America describes roughly 4–20 branches, usually about 5–10 cm long. Panel 3 shows the actual overlapping spikelet rows. A feathery head alone is NOT a secure species ID: inspect a mature detached fertile lemma for the distinctive distal tuft of long fine hairs, separate from its stiff awn. Panel 0 is a HEAD photograph, not a connected rooted plant. New panel 12 shows a species-determined flowering plant still growing in rocky El Paso roadside gravel with multiple upright culms. This is useful regional habitat and growth context, but its roots are hidden: do NOT call it a photographed rooted crown.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FEATHERY TERMINAL HEAD, ONE-SIDED SPIKELETS, REAL TEXAS IN-GROUND HABIT PICTURED; CONNECTED ROOT CROWN NOT EXPOSED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · GROWTH FORM AND TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Dark true stem nodes now photographed; true inner ligule and attached roots still need close-up
field_id_short_tiles.details: Descriptions usually call this a tufted annual with ascending or bent lower stems, sometimes rooting at nodes. The existing ground-level photo (panel 6) shows basal culms converging, NOT exposed roots, independently rooted nodes or proof of lifespan. Panel 2 shows the correct blade/sheath junction but does NOT resolve the true free ligule. Flora of North America reports an erose/ciliate ligule up to about 4 mm, whereas a Southwest treatment describes approximately 0.2–1 mm; keep these treatment-specific values separate. Photograph the opened inner membrane beside a 1-mm ruler and the attached rooted base; do not label pale sheath lips as the ligule. NEW panels 10 and 11 now actually photograph the chestnut-red circumferential STEM NODE on green Chloris virgata culms. Panel 11 also shows the neighboring long green blade and sheath exterior. The dark node is a STEM JOINT, not the blade/sheath collar ligule. The photographic annotation arrows point only to the dark nodes; panel 12 shows a Texas plant in soil but DOES NOT expose or certify roots. The complete inner 0.2–4-mm treatment-variable free membrane still needs a measured face-on photograph.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE DARK STEM NODE PHOTOGRAPHED AND ARROWED; INNER MEMBRANOUS LIGULE / EXPOSED ROOTS STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE MATURE SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: About 2.5–4.5 mm; one fertile plus reduced sterile florets
field_id_short_tiles.details: On one mature unilateral raceme, examine several overlapping spikelets at 10–20×. Flora of North America and diagnostic disseminule treatments describe a spikelet roughly 2.5–4.5 mm long, with one bisexual fertile lower floret and one or sometimes two reduced sterile upper florets. Panels 1 and 3 show real attached units; panels 4, 5 and 7 show detached reproductive units. Do NOT confuse a detached floret unit with a whole spikelet or bare seed. A 0.5-mm scale and one opened same-voucher spikelet are still missing.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL ATTACHED AND DETACHED REPRODUCTIVE UNITS; CALIBRATED INTACT/DISSECTED SPIKELET MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE BOTH GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower about 1.5–2.5 mm; upper about 2.5–4.5 mm
field_id_short_tiles.details: The two basal glumes are unequal, keeled and generally one-veined in Flora of North America, Kew GrassBase and USDA diagnostic treatments. Published lower-glume length is approximately 1.5–2.5 mm and upper approximately 2.5–4.5 mm; the upper tip may taper to a bristlelike point, so do not make an absolute awnless-glume claim. Jim Conrad's panel 4 suggests persistent narrow glumes on the rachis, but no existing image separately measures both or proves each vein. Open a mature specimen and photograph each glume with transmitted light and millimeter scale.
field_id_short_tiles.status: GLUME POSITION SUGGESTED IN PHOTOGRAPH; INDIVIDUAL GLUME LENGTH AND VENATION UNVERIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · HAIR CROWN, FERTILE LEMMA AND TWO AWNS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fine 1.5–4 mm crown hairs are NOT the stiff lemma awns
field_id_short_tiles.details: A fertile lemma body is about 2.5–4 mm in Kew/AusGrass, usually three-veined, with a conspicuous distal fringe/crown of fine hairs approximately 1.5–4 mm. Its distinct subapical awn is reported about 2.5–15 mm in Flora of North America and 5–15 mm in GrassBase. The first sterile upper lemma is reduced (roughly 1.4–3 mm across treatments) and bears its OWN awn, commonly around 3–12 mm; a second very reduced sterile lemma may occur. Panels 5 and 7 genuinely show fine pale hair tufts and two stiff awn shafts, but do NOT resolve their separate attachment points or calibrated lengths. Add no anatomical insertion arrows without dissection.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ACTUAL FINE HAIRS AND TWO AWNS VISIBLE; INDIVIDUAL LEMMA INSERTIONS AND MEASUREMENTS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tiered tumble windmillgrass; hooded windmillgrass; slim radiating windmills
field_id_short_tiles.details: Compared with C. verticillata (OTHER SPECIES panel 9), feather fingergrass commonly crowds its pale feathery racemes near one terminal hub rather than separating long racemes into obvious stem tiers. C. cucullata has short crowded branches and a rounded swollen upper sterile lemma hood; C. andropogonoides has long, relatively slim radiating branches. The source-reported C. × subdolichostachya remains on its scientific hybrid voucher hold; neither parent image nor head silhouette certifies the hybrid. For a confident local ID compare an attached flowering axis, true ligule, paired glumes, fertile hair crown and both awn origins, not color or branch count alone. The new dark-node photos (panels 10–11) add real vegetative anatomy that can distinguish a stem node from the leaf collar; the Texas habitat panel 12 is only growth context, NOT taxonomic proof of lower rooting.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON READY; MATCHED LOCAL VOUCHER DISSECTIONS AND PUBLIC SITE QA MISSING
